anatomy.lede: A small shrimp built around one oversized weapon, with a helmet over its eyes to survive its own blasts.

hotspots.label: Snapper claw
hotspots.text: When this claw snaps shut it fires a water jet fast enough to tear open a cavitation bubble. The bubble's collapse makes the bang that stuns or kills prey.

hotspots.label: Small claw
hotspots.text: The other claw is ordinary-sized. Young shrimps start with two equal claws; one enlarges later, on either side.

hotspots.label: Orbital hood
hotspots.text: A clear, helmet-like extension of the shell covers the eyes. It damps the shock waves from snaps, protecting the shrimp's brain.

hotspots.label: Antennules
hotspots.text: These short feelers sense both chemicals and water movement. Rivals aim fast currents from their gills straight at them during encounters.

hotspots.label: Swimmerets
hotspots.text: Beating the swimmerets drives strong currents backwards, one of several kinds of current the shrimp makes when meeting others.

hotspots.label: Eggs
hotspots.text: This is a female with eggs. In females, a bigger snapper claw comes at a cost: fewer, smaller eggs.

senses.lede: Long thought to be half-blind under its hood, the bigclaw snapping shrimp turns out to see well and to read the water around it.

senses.name: Fast, clear sight
senses.text: Its compound eyes look out through a hood almost as transparent as seawater, resolve detail to about 8 degrees, and have at least two colour classes of photoreceptor.

senses.name: The fastest eyes in water
senses.text: Its eyes sample at least 160 times a second, the fastest yet measured in an aquatic animal, and work from late twilight to direct sunlight.

senses.name: Feeling the jet
senses.text: Hairs on the snapper claw sense the water jet of a rival. When researchers coated them with lacquer, shrimps that were hit retreated instead of approaching.

senses.name: Smelling the current
senses.text: Slow sideways currents from the gills most probably help the shrimp sample odours, and its antennules pick up both chemical and mechanical cues.

body.lede: The snap is a feat of engineering: a spring, a latch and the physics of a collapsing bubble.

systems.title: A spring-loaded claw
systems.text: The snapper claw works by a spring-and-latch mechanism. It develops gradually and starts snapping about a month after hatching, when the claw is only millimetres long.

systems.title: Body armour against blasts
systems.text: Shrimps whose orbital hoods were removed slowed down and lost motor control after shock waves; those with intact hoods did not. It is the first known biological armour that damps shock waves.

systems.title: A costly weapon
systems.text: In three snapping shrimp species, a bigger claw came with a smaller abdomen, suggesting the weapon is paid for with the rest of the body.

mind.lede: Snapping shrimps settle disputes with ritualised shots, water currents and signals rather than all-out fights.

studies.title: Aimed warning shots
studies.text: In staged encounters, a shrimp cocked its claw for about half a second, and over half its snaps were aimed at the rival, usually striking its snapper claw from under a centimetre away. Males held the cock longer and hit more often than females.

studies.title: Talking with water
studies.text: Shrimps fire fast, focused gill currents at an opponent's antennules. Dominant animals released more of these currents and more water jets than subordinates, so the currents may carry information about status.

studies.title: Big claws win partners
studies.text: In males, but not females, a larger snapper claw went with a better chance of being paired and with a relatively larger partner.

survival.lede: Small and soft-bodied, the shrimp relies on its bang and on a good hiding place.

tactics.title: The bang
tactics.text: The snap deters predators as well as stunning prey, and is also used in displays.

tactics.title: Hiding by day
tactics.text: It often hides in a crevice or hole during the day, among reefs, seagrass, salt marshes and mud.

tactics.title: Living in pairs
tactics.text: Most bigclaw snapping shrimps live as monogamous pairs, sharing a shelter.

life.lede: The bigclaw snapping shrimp races through its larval life and starts snapping while still tiny.

stages.name: Mating
stages.text: The female is only receptive for a short time just after she moults.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Eggs hatch about four weeks after being laid.

stages.name: Larva
stages.text: The larvae do not feed but live on their yolk, passing through three larval stages in about five days.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: Reared from eggs, young shrimps began snapping about a month after hatching, as the spring mechanism in the claw gradually developed.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Adults mostly live as monogamous pairs, hiding in crevices and burrows in shallow water.
